title: The kitchen at Amritsar
hookLine: the langar at the Golden Temple feeds tens of thousands every day

lines: ROW AFTER ROW ON THE FLOOR.
cards: The sound comes first: steel plates, stacked and passed and clattering, a rolling metal river of them. Then the smell: lentils, butter, fresh roti.

Then the hall itself, at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, also called the Golden Temple. People sit on long strips of matting, row after row: a farmer, a tourist with a camera, a businessman, a grandmother, a child.
A volunteer walks down the row with a bucket of dal, ladling the same amount onto every plate. Nobody asks who you are.

teach.b: The gurdwara's own accounts say its langar feeds tens of thousands of people every day, and more on festival days. The food is free.
Volunteers do much of the work: kneading dough, rolling roti, stirring huge pots, washing plates. The sitting in rows is called pangat.

teach.h: PANGAT: EVERYONE IN THE SAME ROW.
teach.b: Everyone eats at the same level, the same food, from the same kitchen. There is no head table, and no better plate for an important guest.
Tradition tells that when the emperor Akbar came to meet Guru Amar Das, he was asked to do what everyone did first: sit in the pangat and eat langar.
Sikhs sum up the old rule in a short phrase: pehle pangat, piche sangat.

teach.h: FIRST THE ROW, THEN THE GATHERING.
teach.b: First the row, then the gathering. A ruler of an empire, the story goes, sat on the floor beside whoever was there.
After the meal comes the washing. Visitors line up to scrub steel next to students and farmers. The hands get wrinkled, the plates go back out, and the river keeps flowing.
Tens of thousands fed is not a statistic. It's a meal, multiplied, and every plate given the same.

how: At the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, the langar serves free vegetarian meals to all visitors, who sit together in rows (pangat) on the floor; volunteers cook, serve and wash the dishes as seva.

games.why: pangat: everyone in the same row, at the same level, with the same food. the meal itself says the old dividing lines don't exist here.

practice: Picture the hall and the long mats, and put yourself in the row: a stranger on your left, another on your right, and the plate landing in front of you the same as theirs.
Breathe in, receiving; breathe out, and picture yourself at the sinks, washing someone else's plate. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Pangat. The row where everyone sits together to eat, at the Harmandir Sahib's langar in Amritsar, with free meals served to everyone who comes. Today's word.

orig.note: pangat, the row in which everyone sits together to eat langar.

carryVoice: Your line: tens of thousands fed. That ends a week of Sikh life now: help out of addiction, a turban chosen, the word on screens, honest pictures, a clean river, a forest, and this kitchen. Rest well, and see you tomorrow.
